notes.meaning: Jeroboam's son Abijah became very sick right as the king persisted in false worship. Even royal families face ordinary illness, but this affliction was a divine warning intended to wake Jeroboam up to his sins.

Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to Shiloh to consult the prophet Ahijah, who had originally announced that Jeroboam would be king. In his crisis, the king knew his golden calves were useless and that only the true God had answers. Yet he foolishly believed a prophet who could see into the future could be tricked by a peasant costume.

The queen took simple country foods—ten loaves of bread, sweet cakes, and a jar of honey—to keep up her disguise as a common traveler. Jeroboam only asked to know what would become of his son, treating the prophet like a fortuneteller. Instead of repenting or asking for prayer, he merely wanted to know the future.

Jeroboam's wife obeyed and traveled to Ahijah's house in Shiloh. The aging prophet was physically blind, but his spiritual sight was clear. Even though his eyes could no longer see the light, God continued to give him visions.

The Lord spoke to Ahijah before the woman arrived, warning him that Jeroboam's wife was coming in disguise to ask about her sick child. God gave Ahijah the exact words to say to her. Her human trickery could not hide her identity from the God who knows all things.

As soon as Ahijah heard her footsteps at the door, he called her by name and asked why she was pretending to be someone else. He immediately told her that he had been sent by God with dreadful news. Her disguise fell apart before she could even ask her question.

Ahijah gave the queen a message of judgment for her husband. The Lord reminded Jeroboam that He had raised him up from an ordinary servant and torn the kingdom away from David's dynasty to give it to him. Yet Jeroboam had failed to follow the example of David, who stayed completely loyal to the Lord's worship.

Jeroboam had committed worse evils than any leader before him by making molten calves and idols that provoked God's jealousy. By casting God behind his back, he showed open contempt for the Lord's law and commands. His political religion treated the Almighty as something to be ignored.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars argue that the golden calves were originally meant as symbols or pedestals for the Lord rather than entirely different gods.

notes.meaning: God promised complete and shameful destruction upon Jeroboam's family line, declaring that every male, whether slave or free, would be cut off. His household would be swept away like filthy refuse until nothing remained. Anyone in the family who died in the town would be eaten by stray dogs, and those in the open country would be eaten by birds, leaving them without an honorable burial.

The prophet told the queen to start the long journey home. The moment her feet stepped into the city gate, her sick son would die. The exact timing would serve as a sign that all the other judgments would happen just as God had spoken.

The sick prince would be the only male in the whole family to receive a proper burial and public mourning across Israel. God took him early in mercy because He found genuine devotion toward the Lord in the young prince's heart. Death spared the boy from witnessing and sharing in the terrible ruin of his father's house.

The Lord declared that He was already raising up a future king who would slaughter Jeroboam's entire household. This downfall was not far away; the destroyer was already alive and waiting. This was fulfilled when Baasha murdered the royal family shortly after Jeroboam's death.

Ahijah warned that Israel would be shaken by turmoil like a reed in rough water and eventually uprooted from the promised land. Because the people set up wooden Asherah poles and embraced idols, they would be carried away into exile beyond the Euphrates River. Jeroboam was held responsible not only for his own sins, but also for leading the entire nation into guilt.

Jeroboam's wife returned to the royal residence in Tirzah, and the child died the moment she stepped over the doorway. The nation buried him and wept for him, fulfilling the exact words Ahijah had spoken from the Lord. God's warnings proved completely reliable in every detail.

Jeroboam reigned over northern Israel for twenty-two years, and the details of his reign and border wars were recorded in the public state records. After his death, his son Nadab succeeded him on the throne. Even though he died in office, his dynasty was doomed to fall soon after.

The record turns to the southern kingdom of Judah, where Solomon's son Rehoboam began ruling at age forty-one. He reigned for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the unique city chosen by God for His temple. His mother was Naamah the Ammonite, whose foreign customs brought pagan influences into the royal family.

The people of Judah turned away from God and fell into deep sin. Their betrayal provoked the Lord to jealous anger, just as an unfaithful spouse breaks the sacred marriage covenant. Their offenses were even worse than the rebellion of earlier generations during the period of the judges.

Judah built pagan shrines, sacred stone pillars, and wooden Asherah poles across the land. They carried out these corrupt rituals on every hilltop and under leafy shade trees. Instead of keeping worship pure at the temple, they adopted the superstitious rituals of the surrounding nations.

Pagan shrine prostitutes operated openly in the land as part of idolatrous rites. The people embraced the very abominations for which God had driven out the original Canaanite inhabitants. When true worship is abandoned, moral breakdown quickly follows.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars interpret the Hebrew word for shrine prostitute simply as a cultic priest or temple official rather than someone practicing ritual prostitution.

notes.meaning: In Rehoboam's fifth year, King Shishak of Egypt marched against Jerusalem as God's instrument of judgment. Shishak plundered the treasures of the temple and the royal palace, stripping away the great wealth gathered under David and Solomon. He also carried off all the famous golden shields Solomon had made for ceremonial display.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: A traditional Catholic reading suggests that King Shishak may have launched his invasion of Judah at the invitation of Jeroboam.

notes.meaning: King Rehoboam made cheaper bronze shields to replace the captured gold ones and placed them with the palace gatekeepers. Whenever the king went to the temple, the royal guards marched with the bronze shields and then locked them back in the guardroom. Swapping fine gold for bronze showed how sin drains away the glory and strength of a kingdom.
The rest of Rehoboam's actions and policies were preserved in the royal annals of Judah's kings. These historical records kept an account of his government for future generations to study.

Rehoboam and Jeroboam remained in a state of ongoing conflict and border tension throughout their reigns. Although full-scale conquest had been prevented by God's prophet, deep rivalry kept both kingdoms uneasy.

Rehoboam died and was buried with his royal ancestors in the City of David. The writer mentions again that his mother was Naamah the Ammonite, underlining the foreign pagan influence that shaped his reign. His son Abijam took the throne after him.
